232.title: All this is the Lord's
232.hook: a sage empties out everything he learned, and the sun gives him a page that starts with everything
232.carry: the lord lives in all this
232.howItsDone: Many Hindus know the Isha Upanishad's first verse by heart, and many begin the day looking at their palms with a short verse (karadarshanam) that places Lakshmi, Saraswati and Govinda in their own hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, graduation: the student walked home from the Gita, and your line was speak truth, live dharma, honor the guest as god. Today the path goes underneath the Gita.

Here's how tradition says this week's text arrived. The sage Yajnavalkya, whom you met on day ten, was once the student of a great teacher, Vaishampayana. They quarreled, and the teacher, furious, demanded back everything he'd taught him. So, in the Vishnu Purana's telling, Yajnavalkya threw it up: the whole Yajurveda, right there on the ground. The other students turned into partridges and pecked it up. Then Yajnavalkya, emptied out, prayed to the sun. And the sun came to him as a horse and taught him verses his teacher never knew.
screen: `A SAGE AND AN ANGRY TEACHER.` → `PARTRIDGES.` → `THE SUN, AS A HORSE.`

segments.voice: Those verses became the White Yajurveda, and its closing chapter is the Isha Upanishad: eighteen verses, one page. Upanishad is usually explained as sitting down near, a student close to a teacher. This one is named for its first word, isha, the Lord. And here's the first line: isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is vasyam by the Lord. Some read that word as dwelt in: the Lord lives inside everything, the way salt lives in seawater. The great teacher Shankara read it as clothed: wrap everything you see in the thought of the Lord. Either way, this is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, said plainly. God isn't only in the temple, or up in the sky. God is in all this. It's why many Hindus touch river water to their heads before stepping in, touch a book to the forehead if a foot brushes it, and fold their hands to a stranger. Mahatma Gandhi is often quoted as saying that if every other scripture were lost and only this first verse remained, Hinduism would live on. So where does it meet an ordinary morning? Many Hindus start the day looking at their open palms with a short verse. In the best-known version: Lakshmi lives at the fingertips, Saraswati in the middle, Govinda, Krishna, at the base. Before you've touched your phone, you've seen the sacred in your own two hands.
screen: `THE WHITE YAJURVEDA'S LAST CHAPTER.` · `ISHA: THE LORD.` · `DWELT IN, OR CLOTHED.` · `RIVER, BOOK, STRANGER, YOUR HANDS.` · then, large: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Open your hands in front of you and look at them, the way many Hindus do on waking. If you pray, say the line softly: isha vasyam idam sarvam, all this is the Lord's. Then let your eyes move to whatever is near, a cup, a window, a photo of someone you love, and try the verse on each one. If you don't pray, just look, and let each thing be a little more than ordinary.
Isha, the Lord, the one who rules. Today, the first half of the Isha's first verse: all this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Tomorrow, the renouncing and the enjoying.
Your line: the lord lives in all this. Even in your own two hands. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: Renounce, and enjoy
233.hook: a king says his city can burn and nothing of his will burn
233.howItsDone: Many Hindu families offer food to God before eating and then share it as prasad; some teachers read 'tena tyaktena bhunjitha' in that shape: give it up first, then enjoy it as a gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday, isha: the first half of the first verse. All this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Your line: the lord lives in all this.
screen: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Janaka was the name, or title, of the kings of Mithila; you've met the family before, on day ten and in the Ramayana. The Mahabharata remembers one King Janaka for a single line. He had palaces, cattle, gold and a kingdom to run, and he said, in plain words: my wealth has no end, because nothing is mine. If Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. A king, sitting on everything, saying none of it is his. Not a monk who has walked away. A ruler, still ruling. The second half of the Isha's first verse explains how he could say it.
screen: `KING JANAKA OF MITHILA.` → `NOTHING IS MINE.` → `IF MITHILA BURNS…`

segments.voice: Here's the second half. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Tyakta is let go, given up. Bhunjitha is enjoy, eat, have the use of. They sit side by side, and that's the surprise. Then a warning, ma gridhah, do not covet, and a question: kasya svid dhanam? Whose, really, is wealth? The verse has already answered: the Lord's. This is the Hindu idea of tyaga, renunciation, and it isn't only for monks. Some do leave everything, and they're honored for it. But Janaka stayed king. His letting go was inside: he stopped owning, and kept using, ruling and enjoying, like a trustee, not a proprietor. Some teachers, Gandhi among them, read the verse exactly that way. You can watch the teaching happen in a Hindu kitchen. Many families offer food to God before anyone eats: a plate set before the shrine, a few words, a pause. The food is given away first. Then it comes back as prasad, a gift, and everyone eats it gladly. Renounce, then enjoy. Nobody goes hungry; the meal just stops being something to grab. It works the same with the things that matter most. Hold them as lent, and you can enjoy them with both hands. Grip them as only yours, and you spend the meal guarding the plate.

segments.voice: Before your next drink or meal, pause and offer it, the way many Hindus do. If you pray, say silently, this is yours, or a name of God you love. Then take the first sip or bite as prasad, something given back to you, and notice whether it tastes any different when it isn't simply yours. If you don't pray, just pause, and receive it as a gift.
Tyaktena, by what is let go. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Don't covet. Whose is wealth?
Your line: renounce it, then enjoy it. Janaka let go of owning and kept the kingdom. See you tomorrow.

234.title: Live a hundred years, working
234.hook: a cobbler stays at his bench, and the river reaches out to him
234.carry: work offered to god doesn't bind
234.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Isha verse 2 to show the Upanishads do not require leaving the world; many Hindus honor their tools at Ayudha Puja or Vishwakarma Puja and offer their daily work to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tyaktena: by that renounced, enjoy. Do not covet; whose is wealth? Your line: renounce it, then enjoy it.

In Varanasi, some five or six hundred years ago, lived Ravidas: a leatherworker who mended shoes, and a poet-saint whose songs are still sung, and are also in the Sikh scripture. A well-loved story says his neighbors set off for a festival bath in the Ganga and asked him to come. Ravidas had shoes promised to a customer that day. So he stayed at his bench and handed them a coin: offer this to Mother Ganga for me, but only if she reaches out to take it. At the river, the story says, a hand rose out of the water and took it.
screen: `RAVIDAS, AT HIS BENCH.` → `A COIN FOR THE GANGA.` → `A HAND FROM THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Ravidas is remembered for a saying that grew around it: man changa to kathauti mein Ganga. If the mind is pure, the Ganga is right here in my work bowl. That's the Isha's second verse, lived. Kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah: doing your works here, wish to live a hundred years. Karmani is works, the same karma you met on day seven. A hundred years is the full life the old Vedic prayers ask for. Then the reason: for you, living this way, action does not cling. The word pictures something smeared on, like oil. Work done knowing all this is the Lord's doesn't glue itself to you. This is the root of karma yoga, the Gita's path you spent weeks with: act fully, offer the work, let go of the fruit. And it's why Hinduism honors the householder, the grihastha, who works, raises a family and feeds people, as a real road to God, not a lesser one. You can see it in Hindu life. Once a year, at Ayudha Puja or Vishwakarma Puja, many workshops and homes honor their tools: the sewing machine, the laptop, the truck get kumkum and a flower. Elders bless the young: may you live a hundred years. And plenty of grandmothers will tell you their cooking is their puja. Ravidas didn't need to leave his bench to reach the river. Offered rightly, the work was the river.
screen: `THE GANGA IN MY WORK BOWL.` · `DOING WORKS HERE, LIVE A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `ACTION DOES NOT CLING.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH.` · then, large: `WORK, OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Pick one task waiting for you today: the dishes, a report, a practice session. Before you start, offer it. If you pray, say silently, this is for you, or touch the tool to your forehead, the way many Hindus honor their tools. If you don't pray, dedicate it to someone you love. Then do it well, and when it's done, let it go, like washing oil off your hands.
Karma, action, works. Verse two: doing works here, wish to live a hundred years; action done this way, offered, doesn't cling.
Your line: work offered to god doesn't bind. Ravidas stayed at his bench, and the river came to him. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

235.title: Far, and near
235.hook: a boy finds God in his own heart, opens his eyes, and finds him standing in front of him
235.carry: god is far, and god is near
235.howItsDone: Many Hindu families care for a small murti of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, as a beloved child while worshiping Krishna as Lord of the universe: Isha verse 5's 'far, and near' in one home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma: doing works here, wish to live a hundred years, and the action doesn't cling. Your line: work offered to god doesn't bind.

You met Dhruva on day thirteen: the little prince kept off his father's lap, who walked into the forest to find God. Here's the part of his story that belongs to this week. The Bhagavata Purana says he went so deep in meditation that he saw Vishnu shining in his own heart. Then, suddenly, the form inside him vanished. Dhruva, frightened, opened his eyes. And there, standing in front of him in the forest, was the same Lord he had been seeing within. Inside, and then outside. The same one.
screen: `DHRUVA IN THE FOREST.` → `THE LORD IN HIS HEART.` → `THEN, IN FRONT OF HIM.`

segments.voice: The Isha's verses four and five try to say what Dhruva saw. Verse four: it is one, unmoving, and swifter than the mind; standing still, it outruns those who run. Verse five: tad ejati tan naijati. It moves; it does not move. Tad dure tad v antike. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and outside all this. Why talk in contradictions? Because any single statement would shrink it. Say God is far away, beyond the stars, and you've made God absent from your kitchen. Say God is only right here, and you've made God small enough to fit on a shelf. Hindu teaching holds both: Brahman, beyond every name, and the Lord who lives in your heart and answers to a pet name. Later schools read the verses differently. Shankara's Advaita hears one reality behind every appearance; Ramanuja's line hears a personal Lord living in everything as its inner self, and still more than it. And you can see both in a single Hindu home. In many families a small murti of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, is woken in the morning, bathed, dressed, fed, even given a little sweater in winter. The same family will tell you Krishna is Lord of the whole universe. That isn't a contradiction they've missed. It's the Isha's verse, lived out: far, and near. Swifter than the mind, and close enough to tuck in.
screen: `SWIFTER THAN THE MIND.` · `IT MOVES; IT DOES NOT MOVE.` · `FAR, AND NEAR.` · `BRAHMAN, AND LADDU GOPAL.` · then, large: `TAD DURE TAD V ANTIKE.`

segments.voice: Look out at something vast: the sky through a window, or the thought of the whole earth turning. Let it be far. Then close your eyes and rest a hand on your chest, where Dhruva saw the Lord, and let the same presence be near. If you pray, say a name of God you love, once for far and once for near. If you don't, just hold both: the very big, and the very close.
Ejati, it moves, it stirs. Tad ejati tan naijati: it moves, it does not move; it is far, and it is near, inside all this and outside it.
Your line: god is far, and god is near. Dhruva found him inside, then standing in front of him. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: The self in every being
236.hook: a saint pours the holy water he carried for Shiva into a thirsty donkey
236.howItsDone: Isha verses 6 and 7 are often quoted by Hindu teachers, especially in Vedanta, as the root of seeing one self in every being; many read the greeting namaste, 'I bow to you', in that light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ejati: it moves and does not move, far and near, inside all this and outside it. Your line: god is far, and god is near.

There's a story told about Eknath, a poet-saint of Maharashtra, about four hundred and fifty years ago. He set out with pilgrims carrying water from the holy Ganga, a long walk south, to pour over Shiva at the great temple of Rameshwaram. A pilgrimage of months, and the water was precious. On the road, in the heat, they came upon a donkey lying in the dust, dying of thirst. The others stepped around it. Eknath knelt, opened his pot, and poured the Ganga water into the donkey's mouth. His companions were horrified. That water was for the Lord.
screen: `EKNATH, ON THE ROAD.` → `GANGA WATER FOR SHIVA.` → `A DONKEY, DYING OF THIRST.`

segments.voice: Eknath's answer, as the story is usually told: the Lord just drank it. That's the Isha's sixth verse. The one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not shrink away from anything. The verb is vijugupsate: to recoil, to pull back in disgust. That's the flinch, named. And the cure isn't a rule; it's a way of seeing. Hindus call the self within atman, and this verse says the same self looks out of every face. Pulling away from someone becomes like pulling away from your own hand. Verse seven asks: for the one who sees oneness, ekatvam, what delusion is there, what sorrow? Verse eight praises the one who pervades all this: bright, bodiless, without wound, pure. You met this in the Gita too, where the wise see the same in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person everyone else cast out. Here's where it meets a day. The everyday Hindu greeting, namaste, means I bow to you, and many teachers read it as the divine in me bowing to the divine in you. At many temples, prasad goes to everyone in the line, the rich man and the man who slept outside. Seeing this way doesn't erase differences, and it doesn't mean staying near someone who hurts you. It means the recoil loses its ground, because there's nobody there who isn't carrying the Lord.
screen: `THE LORD JUST DRANK IT.` · `ALL BEINGS IN THE SELF.` · `NO LONGER SHRINKING BACK.` · `NAMASTE.` · then, large: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone mildly hard to be near, not the hardest person in your life, and notice the small pull back in your jaw or shoulders. Then fold your hands, the way you would for namaste. If you pray, say silently: the same Lord is in you. If you don't, try: the same life breathing in me is breathing in you. See if the flinch softens a little; if it doesn't, that's fine, you looked.
Ekatva, oneness. For the one who sees oneness, what delusion is there, what sorrow? See all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, and stop shrinking back.
Your line: one self in every being. Eknath saw the Lord drink from a donkey's mouth. Until tomorrow.

237.title: Knowing and doing
237.hook: Arjuna begs Krishna to just pick one, and the Isha refuses too
237.tomorrow: The face of truth, covered in gold
237.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of different schools read Isha verses 9–14 differently, but the verses are commonly taught as a call to hold inner knowledge and outer action together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekatva, oneness. See all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, and one self in every being. Your line: one self in every being.

Remember Arjuna in the chariot. Krishna has praised knowledge, the quiet wisdom that sees the self. Then he's praised action, doing your duty. And at the start of chapter three, Arjuna says what every confused student says: if knowledge is better than action, why push me into this terrible work? You're mixing me up. Tell me the one thing, for certain. In chapter five he tries again: you praise giving up action, then you praise doing it. Which is better? Just pick one. Krishna's answer: only children talk as if the two are different. The wise see them as one.
screen: `ARJUNA: JUST PICK ONE.` → `KNOWLEDGE, OR ACTION?` → `THE WISE SEE THEM AS ONE.`

segments.voice: The Isha makes the same refusal, in its own strange way. Verse nine: into blind darkness go those who follow avidya, not-knowing. Into a greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in vidya, knowing, alone. Knowledge on its own gets the worse darkness. What do the words mean here? The text doesn't define them, and scholars still argue. Shankara took vidya as meditation, inner knowing, and avidya as ritual and work in the world. However you read them, verse eleven says what to do: the one who knows both together crosses death by the one and reaches the deathless by the other. Verses twelve to fourteen run the same pattern with another pair. This is a big Hindu teaching: wisdom and practice belong together. Jnana, knowing, and karma, doing, aren't rival teams. You can see it in an ordinary Hindu evening. Someone lights the lamp and waves it for aarti: the hands, doing. And the same person may know what many say the flame means: light offered back to the source of light. Without the knowing, a ritual can go hollow. Without the doing, knowing floats off and gets proud, which may be why the Isha gives knowledge alone the darker place. Arjuna wanted one answer. Both texts give him two, held in one hand.
screen: `BLIND DARKNESS: NOT-KNOWING ALONE.` · `GREATER DARKNESS: KNOWING ALONE.` · `KNOW BOTH TOGETHER.` · `THE LAMP, AND WHAT IT MEANS.` · then, large: `VIDYA AND AVIDYA, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you have a lamp, a candle or a diya, light it, or just picture one: that's the doing. Then say, aloud or inside, one line you've learned this week, maybe isha vasyam idam sarvam: that's the knowing. Hold the two together for a few breaths, the flame and its meaning. If you don't pray, let the light be a small act of care, and the line a thought to carry with it.
Vidya, knowledge, from vid, to know. The one who knows vidya and avidya together crosses death and gains the deathless; follow only one and it goes dark.
Your line: knowing and doing, held together. Either one alone goes dark. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

238.title: The face of truth, covered in gold
238.hook: an old warrior waits for the sun, and the Isha ends with a prayer for the last walk
238.carry: uncover it, so I may see
238.howItsDone: Isha verses 15–18 are recited at some Hindu funerals and at the bedside of the dying; verse 18, the prayer to Agni to lead by the good path, also appears in the Rig Veda (1.189.1).

segments.voice: Yesterday, vidya and avidya: the lamp and what it means, knowing and doing, held together. Either one alone goes dark.

At the end of the great war, the old warrior Bhishma lies on a bed of arrows. He has the gift of choosing when he dies, and the Mahabharata says he chooses to wait for the sun to turn north, the season held most auspicious for leaving the body. Fifty-eight nights he lies there, teaching the Pandavas, and watching the sun. A dying man, waiting for light. The Isha ends at that kind of moment. After a week of teaching, it stops explaining, turns to the sun, and prays.
screen: `BHISHMA ON THE ARROWS.` → `WAITING FOR THE SUN.` → `THE ISHA PRAYS.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen: hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc, like a lid. The speaker turns to Pushan, the nourisher, a name for the sun: uncover it, so that I, whose way is truth, may see. Notice the lid isn't ugly. It's gold. What hides the truth is often something lovely: praise, comfort, the shine of what we own. Verse sixteen: spread out your rays, gather in your light, so I can see your most blessed form. Then a startling line: that person there, I am he. The one behind the gold isn't a stranger. Verse seventeen is spoken at the edge of death: the breath goes back to the immortal wind, and this body ends in ashes. Om, mind, remember; remember what was done. And verse eighteen turns to Agni, fire: lead us by the good path, you who know all our ways; take the crooked wrong away from us. This is how Hinduism meets a death: with a prayer to be led. Some families say these verses at a bedside, and at the cremation the body is given to Agni, the fire this verse asks for guidance. And remember who gave Yajnavalkya this Veda: the sun. The week began with the sun's gift and ends with a prayer to it. All this is the Lord's. Renounce, and enjoy. Work, offered. Far, and near. One self in every being. Knowing and doing. Uncover it, so I may see.
screen: `THE FACE OF TRUTH, COVERED WITH GOLD.` · `UNCOVER IT, SO I MAY SEE.` · `MIND, REMEMBER.` · `AGNI: LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.` · then, large: `ISHA.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what the golden lid in your life is right now: something good, even lovely, that might be keeping you from seeing what's true; you don't have to remove it, just name it quietly. Then breathe, and on each out-breath imagine the lid lifting a little. If you pray, you can say the verse's own request in your own language, uncover it, so I may see; otherwise, just watch the breath.
Hiranmaya, golden, made of gold. The face of truth is covered with a golden disc; Pushan, the sun, is asked to uncover it, so the truthful may see.
Your line: uncover it, so I may see. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad that starts with a child's question. That's the whole Isha, and day two hundred thirty-eight.
